source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction gains in earlier papers used the true answer label to decide when to stop. With that oracle, accuracy rises.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 82.0, HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0. GPT-4 with oracle: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: Gains come from the outside check, not from reflection. Matches G2.
agent_relevance: Revise (S5) only when code or a test says the output is wrong.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without the oracle, asking the model to review and fix its own answer lowers accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (3 calls) and 41.8 (5 calls). GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43.
quote: without the use of oracle labels, self-correction consistently results in a decrease in performance
limits: Same-model feedback only. Tasks are reasoning QA, not open-ended design.
agent_relevance: Do not add an unaided reflection pass (SCHEMA 4b).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: The model mostly keeps its answer, but when it changes, it breaks right answers more often than it fixes wrong ones.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 74.7% of answers kept after two rounds; among changes, more went correct to wrong than wrong to correct. On CommonSenseQA it changes more, because wrong options look plausible.
limits: Stated mechanism: the model cannot judge the correctness of its own reasoning.
agent_relevance: A revise step needs an external correctness signal, or it adds noise.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: The drop is not only a weak-model problem. GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2 also lose accuracy; the weaker model loses most.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0; CommonSenseQA 84.0 to 81.5 to 83.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5 to 36.5; CommonSenseQA 64.0 to 37.5 to 36.5.
limits: Prompts were fixed critique prompts; other prompts also failed (Tables 5, 6).
agent_relevance: Blind revise costs more on small models.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Self-refine helps on open-ended tasks with many ways to miss a goal: dialogue, constrained generation, readability, acronyms.
numbers: GPT-4 dialogue preference 25.4% to 74.6%. Constrained generation 28.0 to 37.0 (+9.0). GPT-4 code optimization 27.3 to 36.0 (+8.7). Abstract: about 20% absolute gain on average over 7 tasks.
limits: Several tasks are scored by GPT-4 preference (agreement with humans 82%, 68%, 71% on three tasks). Preference judging is weak (G8). No outside-check control against resampling.
agent_relevance: Reflection pays where there is a concrete checklist (concepts covered). Closer to design than math is, but the judge problem remains.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: On math reasoning, self-refine gives no gain. The model cannot spot its error.
numbers: Math reasoning 64.1 to 64.1 (0 change). For ChatGPT, feedback on 94% of instances was 'everything looks good'.
quote: a consistent-looking reasoning chain can deceive LLMs
limits: Appendix variant with outside feedback lifted math from 24.18 to 40.5.
agent_relevance: Where answers are checkable, the check must be code, not text.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion writes a lesson after each failed trial. The success signal comes from the environment (task failure, tests), not from the model's opinion.
numbers: ALFWorld, 134 tasks: ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 within 12 trials; ReAct alone stalled between trials 6 and 7. Abstract: +22% ALFWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over strong baselines.
limits: The trial signal is binary and external. A heuristic detector for hallucination and inefficient plans also helped.
agent_relevance: Nearest LLM model of reflection-in-action as a loop: act, get situation feedback, write a lesson, retry. Keep feedback external.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion is not a win everywhere. On Leetcode Hard (Python) it scored below GPT-4 alone.
numbers: HumanEval Python: GPT-4 80.1 to Reflexion 91.0. Leetcode Hard Python: GPT-4 80.1 vs Reflexion 77.1.
limits: Self-generated tests can pass falsely, so the feedback is itself noisy.
agent_relevance: Self-written tests are weak outside checks (G3 needs held-out checks).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Finding the error step is the bottleneck, not fixing it. Models are poor at locating mistakes in chain-of-thought.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 2186 traces, 5 tasks. GPT-4 best overall at 52.87 accuracy with direct step-level prompting. GPT-3.5-Turbo far lower. Trace-level 'is it right' prompts do better on wrong traces but worse on correct ones.
limits: Traces come from PaLM 2; five algorithmic tasks.
agent_relevance: Talking back to the situation needs a locator: code that says which step failed.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Given the true error location, backtracking fixes many wrong answers. A random location helps wrong traces less and harms correct ones.
numbers: Gain on originally-wrong traces with true location: +18.04 to +43.92 points (multistep arithmetic +43.92). Random location: +5.16 to +21.57. On originally-correct traces, true location: 0 to -11.43; random: -8.89 to -15.91.
limits: Few correct traces per task (45 in some).
agent_relevance: A revision aimed at the wrong place costs correct work. Gate revise on a located failure.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey result: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM except in tasks exceptionally suited to it. It works with reliable external feedback. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Critical survey of the self-correction literature, with a checklist for fair experiments. Many studies lack a defined research question or use unfair oracle or tool feedback.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Review, no new experiment.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and the 4b ban on unaided reflection.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompting alone fails but training with RL on the model's own correction attempts gives real gains.
numbers: Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash: SCoRe improves self-correction by 15.6% on MATH and 9.1% on HumanEval (absolute).
limits: Needs training; our agent cannot train.
agent_relevance: What helps is trained, so a scaffold cannot copy it with a prompt.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Critique that calls outside tools (search, code interpreter, toxicity API) works. The same loop without tools gives small or negative change.
numbers: ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 across three QA tasks, +7.0% absolute on three math tasks, 79.2% lower toxicity probability.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Tool access is the active ingredient.
agent_relevance: Let the situation talk back through tools and execution.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: On graph coloring, GPT-4 critiquing itself did far worse than no critique. Its own verifier missed true solutions and invented errors.
numbers: No backprompts: 16% (100 instances). Backprompting with same-model verifier feedback: 1 of 100 correct. Sound external verifier helped; plain resampling at n=15, t=1.0 reached about 40%, equal to backprompting.
limits: One domain (graph coloring).
agent_relevance: Resampling matches reflection at equal cost, as G4 and G11 imply.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Effects on Problem-Solving Performance
finding: A positive result with a big caveat: reflection helps when the agent already knows its first answer was wrong.
numbers: Nine LLMs, 1000 questions (10 exams x 100). GPT-4 on initially-wrong items: baseline 0.786, Retry (told only that it was wrong) 0.827, Explanation 0.876, Solution 0.925, Composite 0.932, Unredacted (answer leaked) 0.971. All p<0.001 (McNemar).
quote: even the mere knowledge that the agent previously made a mistake improves the agent's performance
limits: Only wrong items are reflected on, so the wrong/right flag is an oracle. Part of the gain is the Retry effect (+0.041). Rich reflections give indirect guidance toward the answer. Largest gain on LSAT analytic reasoning, small on SAT English.
agent_relevance: The error flag carries part of the gain. Needs a real signal.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Effects on Problem-Solving Performance
finding: The same pattern holds in every model tested, and gain grows with how much the reflection says.
numbers: Claude 3 Opus 0.792 to 0.849 (Retry) to 0.947 (Composite). Gemini 1.0 Pro 0.617 to 0.724 to 0.774. Cohere Command R+ 0.641 to 0.745 to 0.874. Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.751 to 0.813 to 0.815.
limits: Content-rich reflections beat terse ones (keywords, advice).
agent_relevance: If we store a reflection, tie it to the located failure.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction
finding: Intrinsic self-correction makes models change answers too often, including right ones. Weak models lose most.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B on a complex task: accuracy down 20.4 points with 58.8% of correct answers overturned. GPT-3.5-turbo changes its final answer more than 6 times in 10 rounds for 81.3% of questions.
limits: Triggers tested include 'Are you sure?' and 'You are wrong'.
agent_relevance: A reflection prompt pushes the model toward changing. Mark as a risk.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction
finding: The authors name three failure patterns that mirror human biases: overthinking, cognitive overload, perfectionism.
numbers: Decision-making failures: perfectionism bias 49.0%, cognitive overload 33.3%, overthinking 17.6%. Internal answer changed 14.1% of the time with self-correction vs 8.3% at first generation (Llama probing).
limits: Taxonomy; labelling partly model-assisted.
agent_relevance: Cap rounds. A second look should not run on a schedule (G1).

source: Suwa, Tversky, Gero, Purcell (2001) Seeing into sketches: regrouping parts encourages new interpretations
finding: Protocol analysis of one experienced architect designing a museum. He often looked at his own sketch in a new grouping, and regrouping went with spotting unintended features. This is the lowest-level evidence for the sketch 'talking back'.
numbers: 340 segments: new grouping 136 (40%), previous grouping 182 (54%), no revisiting 22 (6%). 606 perceptual actions; 171 (28%) were detection of unintended features.
limits: Single expert, retrospective protocol, one coder for the main analysis; correlational, not causal.
agent_relevance: The useful move is re-seeing the same artifact in a different grouping, not general self-critique.

source: Suwa, Tversky, Gero, Purcell (2001) Seeing into sketches: regrouping parts encourages new interpretations
finding: Novice experiment on four ambiguous line drawings: people who attended to parts made about twice as many interpretations, and their rate of new ideas decayed more slowly.
numbers: 36 participants in three self-selected groups. Mean interpretations: No Parts (n=13) 27.2 (SD 12.2); Different Parts (n=12) 44.6 (SD 12.0); Regroup Parts (n=11) 49.6 (SD 30.4). Different vs No: F(1,23)=12.9, p<.01. Regroup vs No: F(1,22)=5.96, p<.05. Different vs Regroup: F(1,21)=0.27. Decay of rate lower in Different Parts F=11.5 and Regroup Parts F=24.3, p<.01.
limits: Groups formed by reported strategy, not assignment: 7 told to regroup could not, and 12 in the attend-only group invented it. Self-selection confounds ability and strategy. No drawing effect, chi2(3)=5.02, p>.1.
agent_relevance: Telling a solver to look at parts differently is a cheap lever for new readings; an agent can re-parse an artifact.

source: Suwa, Gero, Purcell (2000) Unexpected discoveries and S-invention of design requirements (search summary only)
finding: From a search summary, not read: protocol study of one practising architect; about half the process showed two-way links between unexpected discoveries and invention of new requirements.
numbers: Summary says 608 perceptual actions and 173 unexpected discoveries (28.5%). The 2001 paper reports 606 and 171 (28%) for the related analysis, so exact counts differ by version.
limits: Not opened. Single architect.
agent_relevance: Use only as pointer; cite the 2001 counts.

source: Mangano, LaToza, Petre, van der Hoek (2015) How Software Designers Interact with Sketches at the Whiteboard
finding: Eight pairs of professional software designers at a whiteboard. Sketches carry the design conversation; reasoning (mental simulation, review of progress, alternatives) mostly used sketches but left no trace.
numbers: 14 hours, 8 pairs, over 4000 coded events. Over 80% of reasoning activities made use of sketches. Designers rarely worked with one sketch for more than 30 seconds. Coder agreement 80.0%, 82.4%, 78.6% on three codings.
limits: One task (traffic simulator), observational, no outcome quality measure. Schön cited only as background.
agent_relevance: In software work much talk-back is quick shifts across several artifacts. Keep several views, not one.

source: Mejia, Arango, Chan (2018) Unexpected discoveries and their enhancement of the design process
finding: Two-student protocol comparison of parametric versus geometric digital modelling. Unexpected discoveries were few and a link to creativity of outcome could not be tested.
numbers: Two protocols of 81 segments each; 113.5 vs 99.4 minutes. Unexpected discoveries: 2 (parametric) vs 3 (geometric). Eight judges scored novelty, resolution, elaboration, 1 to 5. Coder segmentation similarity 62% and 71%.
limits: N=2. No statistics. Coders agreed on segmenting only about two thirds of the time.
agent_relevance: Shows how thin human evidence for discovery-driven revision is beyond Suwa's single architect.

source: Kokotovich (2015) A Case for Reimagining Reflection-in-Action and Co-evolution
finding: Conceptual critique. Reflection-in-action leans on past experience and tacit, spontaneous responses and may narrow the issues considered. Fix offered: map the problem space before solution work.
numbers: IASDR 2015, pp. 1115-1128. No data reported in the record. Builds on Maher and Poon 1996 and Dorst and Cross 2001.
limits: Only the abstract record was read, not the full paper. Position paper, not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: A loop built on past cases may narrow. Add problem mapping before revision (links to framing subfield).

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: Backprompting gains were matched by plain resampling. Self-critique is no better than drawing more samples.
numbers: Sampling n=5 close but below; n=15 at t=1.0 about 40%, same as all four backprompt types (about 40%) on graph coloring, from a 16% single-pass baseline.
limits: One task family. Verifier quality drives the result.
agent_relevance: Supports G4/G11: several short independent attempts before any reflective pass.
